---
title: Quickstart
description: Embed a dataset with polars-umap in a few lines and plot the result.
jupyter: python3
---

This page takes you from a DataFrame of high-dimensional vectors to a 2D map of them. We'll use
the handwritten digits that ship with scikit-learn: 1,797 images of 8×8 pixels, so 64 numbers
per image.

## Load the data

```{python}
import polars as pl
import polars_umap as pu  # registers the `umap` namespace
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
digits = pl.DataFrame({"pixels": X, "digit": y})
digits.head()
```

The 2D NumPy array becomes an `Array(Float64, 64)` column: one fixed-length vector per row. This
is how embeddings usually live in Polars.

## Run UMAP

Call `.umap.fit_transform()` on the column:

```{python}
digits = digits.with_columns(
    xy=pl.col("pixels").umap.fit_transform(random_state=42),
)
digits.head()
```

The result is an `Array(Float32, 2)` column with one 2D point per row. `random_state` makes the
result reproducible: run it again and you get exactly the same numbers.

If you'd rather have one column per dimension, use the DataFrame helper:

```{python}
digits = digits.umap.fit_transform("pixels", random_state=42)
digits.select("digit", "umap_0", "umap_1").head()
```

## Plot it

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: Show the plotting code
import altair as alt

centers = digits.group_by("digit").agg(pl.col("umap_0", "umap_1").median())
points = (
    alt.Chart(digits.select("digit", "umap_0", "umap_1"))
    .mark_circle(size=12, opacity=0.5, color="#8d8b86")
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("umap_0", axis=None),
        y=alt.Y("umap_1", axis=None),
        tooltip=[alt.Tooltip("digit:N", title="Digit")],
    )
)
labels = (
    alt.Chart(centers)
    .mark_text(fontSize=16, fontWeight="bold", color="#5f5d58")
    .encode(x="umap_0", y="umap_1", text="digit:N")
)
(points + labels).properties(width="container", height=440).configure_view(stroke=None)
```

UMAP has never seen the labels, yet each digit forms its own cluster. Digits that are easy to
confuse, such as 1 and 7, or 3, 5 and 8, end up closer together.
